units.translation: The stain of murder is compounded with time.
I will establish this ordinance for all time.
For time flowing on will be more precious to these citizens.
And will he give me a pledge for all time?
and heavy upon you for all time.
But not for long will my father leave me desolate,
And there is no length of time in between.
an unknown crowd, to be tested by time.
And after that he drank beer, wasting away with time.
For time has no limit to toil.
In time this expedition captures the city of Priam.
The Erinyes, in time, make dim the fortunate man.
You will learn by inquiring in time.
And the renowned deep-thinking Erinys brings a child into the house to pay for the pollution of older bloodshed in time.
Justice came to the sons of Priam in time.
In time, indeed, and on the appointed day, he will pay the penalty.
these things need a long speech
these things need a long speech to be explained clearly
It remains, while Zeus remains, in time for the doer to suffer.
your father will leave you desolate for long

Improperly, Mars, who exchanges the bodies of the slain for ashes, i.e. who gives ashes in return for bodies, as Wellauer interprets it. The word is not found in other authors, but is noted by Hesychius, who explains it by ἀργυρογνώμων [one who knows silver].
But Ares, the gold-exchanger, sends to the loved ones of the bodies a small dust,
and the contracted form χρυσοῦς, about which I have spoken in Thes. vol. 8 p. 1719, golden.
And he speaks with golden letters.
with silver-wrought horns and golden mouthpieces attached.

where the errors of the copies are χρυσεοστόλους χρυσεοστόλβους χρυσεοστίλβους [gold-robed, gold-gleaming, gold-glittering]. Aeschylus used the noun στολμός [equipment, array] twice, Ch. 29 and Suppl. 715. Euripides, however, in Herc.f. 414 said πέπλων χρυσεόστολον φάρος [a gold-adorned robe of cloth].
Chrysean, a gentile adjective from Χρύση, which was a city of the Troad, or another of the same name: for there were several, about which see Thes. vol. 8 p. 1724.
a leader of the Persians. Wrongly Thomas Magister took Χρυσεύς as a proper name and Μάταλλος as an epithet. With the name Μάταλλος Weilius compared Ματίλλας on an Ephesian coin in Mionnet. 3 p. 87.
Chryseus Matalus, commander of ten thousand,
Chryseis, daughter of Chryses, known from Homer, whose proper name was Ἀστυνόμη, as the Homeric scholiast notes on Il. 1, 392.
In the plural number, to signify girls such as Chryseis was.
a delight of Chryseis-like girls from those under Ilium.
